thesis.claim: Evolution in B2 does not learn to resist the raider. In B2's worlds played on to 10,000 iterations, patches of 5% of raiders take hold as often at iterations 5,000 and 10,000 as at 500 and 2,000: a one-sided Fisher exact test finds no fewer late than early at the 5% level. A planting takes hold as in Experiment 29: after 300 iterations its raiders are alive, more than the patch began with, and more than the control patch of residents holds there.
thesis.why: In every long world the book has, an agent's best reply to the rest would gain about one node a game, as much at 50,000 iterations as at 2,500 (Chapter 95): evolution does not close in on any equilibrium. The raider exploits what B2's brains do not do, and nothing in a world that has never met a raider selects against one. Later brains beat earlier ones by less and less, which a world learning to defend itself would not show.
thesis.confirm: The plantings that take hold at 5,000 and 10,000 together (30, in five worlds at three places each) are not fewer than at 500 and 2,000 together by a one-sided Fisher exact test at the 5% level.
thesis.refute: Fewer take hold late than early by that test: evolution closed the door. The chapter then asks what opened instead (other raids that later brains lose to) or whether nothing did.
